promise_quote: WFIRST is a wide-field-of-view near-infrared imaging and low-resolution spectroscopy observatory that will tackle two of the most fundamental questions in astrophysics: Why is the expansion rate of the universe accelerating? And are there other solar systems like ours, with worlds like Earth?
science_question: Determine why the expansion rate of the universe is accelerating and how common Earth-like planets are, via a microlensing exoplanet census combined with weak-lensing, baryon-acoustic-oscillation, and supernova dark-energy measurements.
source_locator: p. 8, Table ES.5; p. 205, Priority 1 (Large, Space)
rationale: Table ES.5 lists WFIRST as a NASA/DOE collaboration; total appraised cost and U.S. share are both $1.6B (DOE contributes the JDEM-Omega design heritage; NASA leads). Committee's top space priority; recommends a 2013 new start to enable a 2020 launch (p. 208).

promise_quote: The Explorer program’s Small Explorer (SMEX) and Medium-scale Explorer (MIDEX) missions, developed and launched on few-year timescales, enable rapid response to new discoveries and provide platforms for targeted investigations essential to the breadth of NASA’s astrophysics program.
science_question: Sustain a steady cadence of competitively selected, rapidly developed small and medium missions (2 MIDEX, 2 SMEX, 4 Missions of Opportunity over the decade) so the program can respond quickly to new astrophysics discoveries and technical breakthroughs.
source_locator: p. 8, Table ES.5; p. 208, Priority 2 (Large, Space)
rationale: Table ES.5 lists Launch Date as 'Ongoing' (not a discrete year), so target_date is left null. Total and U.S. share both $463M, funding the augmentation to raise the astrophysics Explorer budget from ~$40M/year to ~$100M/year by 2015. Entirely a NASA program.

promise_quote: LISA is a gravity wave observatory that would open an entirely new window in the universe.
science_question: Directly detect and measure the full gravitational waveform from mergers of black holes with masses from 10,000 to 10 million solar masses, and census Milky Way compact binaries, to precisely test general relativity.
source_locator: p. 8, Table ES.5; p. 209, Priority 3 (Large, Space)
rationale: Table ES.5: total appraised cost $2.4B, with NASA's ~50% share appraised at $1.5B (70% confidence) and U.S. spending of $852M in 2012-2021. Requires ESA partnership and a successful LISA Pathfinder mission (launch then scheduled 2012); recommendation contingent on those two decision points, with a 2016 new start enabling a mid-2020s launch.

promise_quote: IXO is a versatile large-area, high-spectral-resolution X-ray observatory.
science_question: Use large-aperture, high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy to trace how the first massive black holes form and grow and how hot gas cycles through and around galaxies and clusters, and to test relativistic accretion physics near black holes and neutron stars.
source_locator: p. 8, Table ES.5; p. 213, Priority 4 (Large, Space)
rationale: Table ES.5: total appraised cost $5.0B, U.S. (NASA) share $3.1B, with $200M planned for U.S. spending in 2012-2021 (mostly technology development). Joint NASA/ESA/JAXA mission. Table lists Launch Date as '2020s' with no early/mid/late qualifier, so mapped to the full decade. Ranked 4th large space priority reflecting technical/cost/programmatic uncertainty; NASA cost capped at $2B via descopes if needed.

promise_quote: The ultimate goal is to image rocky planets that lie in the habitable zone of nearby stars—at a distance from their star where water can exist in liquid form—and to characterize their atmospheres.
science_question: Determine what fraction of nearby stars host Earth-like rocky planets in the habitable zone and characterize zodiacal-light levels, to lay the technology and target-selection groundwork for a future direct-imaging mission.
source_locator: p. 7, Table ES.4; p. 215, Priority 1 (Medium, Space)
rationale: Table ES.4 title frames this as preparation 'for a 2020 Decade Mission' and text says the direct-detection mission itself could start 'early in the 2020 decade,' but the technology-development program's own timing is described only as an early-decade $4M/year start with a mid-decade DSIAC review and a possible late-decade ramp to a notional $100M (range $100M-$200M) -- no single decade-quadrant term applies, so target_date is left null; marked guess because the mapping to this report's date convention is not clean. Cost is committee-generated, FY2010 dollars, entirely NASA-funded.

promise_quote: Detecting the B-mode polarization pattern on the cosmic microwave background impressed by gravitational waves produced during the first few moments of the universe both would provide strong evidence for the theory of inflation that is so crucial to our understanding of how structures form, and would open a new window on exotic physics in the early universe in regimes not accessible even to the most powerful particle accelerators on Earth.
science_question: Detect the B-mode polarization signature of primordial gravitational waves in the cosmic microwave background as evidence for cosmic inflation, and develop the technology for a possible dedicated CMB space mission.
source_locator: p. 7, Table ES.4; p. 217, Priority 2 (Medium, Space)
rationale: Table ES.4 frames this as preparation for 'a possible mission beyond 2020'; the program itself proceeds at a modest early-decade level via suborbital/Explorer opportunities, with a notional $60M (range $60M-$200M) mission-specific effort triggered only if B-modes are detected mid-decade -- no clean early/mid/late decade term applies, so target_date is null and confidence marked guess. Entirely NASA-funded, FY2010 committee-generated cost.

promise_quote: The Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) would employ the most ambitious optical sky survey approach yet and would revolutionize investigations of transient phenomena.
science_question: Use repeated wide-field optical imaging (weak gravitational lensing and Type Ia supernovae) to determine why the expansion rate of the universe is accelerating, while also mapping the time-variable sky.
source_locator: p. 6, Table ES.3; p. 223, Priority 1 (Large, Ground)
rationale: Table ES.3: appraised construction cost $465M, U.S. federal share $421M (two-thirds NSF MREFC, one-quarter DOE MIE funds). Top-ranked ground priority; Table ES.3 gives 'Science late 2010s', mapped per report convention to 2016-2019.

promise_quote: The committee recommends, as its second-highest priority, a competed program, based on NASA’s highly successful Explorer model, that would enable moderate-scale projects to be frequently selected through peer review.
science_question: Provide a competitively selected, peer-reviewed funding line (targeting at least seven projects over the decade) for moderate-scale ground-based instrumentation and facility projects between NSF's MRI (<$4M) and MREFC (>$135M) thresholds.
source_locator: p. 6, Table ES.3; p. 225, Priority 2 (Large, Ground)
rationale: Table ES.3 footnote a notes this augmentation's cost is committee-generated (not CATE-derived) but still in FY2010 dollars: building to $40M/year by mid-decade, for $93M-$200M in additional decade funding. Table ES.3 gives 'Science mid-to-late 2010s', mapped directly per the report convention to 2013-2019. NSF-AST program; no DOE/NASA role stated.

promise_quote: These Giant Segmented Mirror Telescopes (GSMTs) will be essential to understanding the distant galaxies discovered by JWST and to obtaining spectra of the faint transients found by LSST, and they will be transformative for a broad range of science aimed at understanding targets ranging from stars and exoplanets to black holes.
science_question: Use high-spatial- and high-spectral-resolution optical/near-infrared spectroscopy on a 20- to 40-meter segmented-mirror telescope to determine the masses and chemical buildup of the earliest galaxies found by JWST and to directly image exoplanet systems.
source_locator: p. 6, Table ES.3; p. 228, Priority 3 (Large, Ground)
rationale: Table ES.3: appraised construction cost $1.1B (GMT) to $1.4B (TMT), with U.S. federal share $257M-$350M targeted at a ~25% partnership share in one of the two U.S.-led projects (GMT or TMT); NSF is the funding agency (MREFC + operations). Table ES.3 gives 'Science mid-2020s', mapped per report convention to 2023-2026.

promise_quote: A new ACTA would be roughly 10 times more sensitive than existing facilities and able to further constrain the nature of dark matter.
science_question: Use a ~1-square-kilometer array of Cerenkov telescopes, roughly 10 times more sensitive than existing arrays, to indirectly detect dark matter via gamma-ray annihilation/decay signatures and to study particle acceleration near active galactic nuclei.
source_locator: p. 7, Table ES.3; p. 232, Priority 4 (Large, Ground)
rationale: Table ES.3: total appraised cost $400M, U.S. federal share $100M (notional, split among DOE, NSF-AST, and NSF-PHY), as a minority partner joining the European CTA project. Table ES.3 gives 'Science early 2020s', mapped per report convention to the first four years of the 2020s (2020-2023).

promise_quote: With a broad scientific agenda, CCAT will enable studies of the evolution of galaxies across cosmic time, the formation of clusters of galaxies, the formation of stars in the Milky Way, the formation and evolution of planets, and the nature of objects in the outer solar system.
science_question: Conduct wide-field submillimeter (200 micron-2 mm) surveys, with 200 times ALMA's field of view, to identify dusty high-redshift galaxies and survey star and planet formation and outer solar-system objects as an essential complement to ALMA.
source_locator: p. 6, Table ES.2; p. 234, Priority 1 (Medium, Ground)
rationale: Table ES.2: total appraised construction cost $140M, of which NSF plans to fund $37M (about a third; project is otherwise university-led/privately funded), plus a possible $7.5M NSF share of $11M annual operations. Table ES.2 gives 'Science early 2020s', mapped per report convention to 2020-2023.

promise_quote: It addresses many of this report’s identified science goals, especially understanding the birth of galaxies, stars, and planets as well as the cycling of matter through our own interstellar medium and dusty gas in nearby galaxies.
science_question: Use a cooled 3.5-meter mid- and far-infrared (5-210 micron) telescope to study how galaxies, stars, and planets form and how matter cycles through the interstellar medium.
source_locator: p. 5, Table ES.1; p. 218, U.S. Contribution to the JAXA-ESA SPICA Mission
rationale: Named JAXA-led mission with ESA/US participation; Table ES.1 lists a $150M notional NASA budget including operations over the decade, for U.S. contribution of infrared instrumentation. Planned launch date given in the text as 2018.
